items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' confirmation. The call opened 'Hey, this is Jack with Einstein Moving Company company. Is this anna?' and went straight into untangling her two submissions — no roadmap, no timeframe. Jack did sense-check twice later ('Any questions about the pricing process or anything like that?', 'Does that work for you?'), but never set the agenda up front.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up question — he moved directly to the record cleanup.

No stairs question at either address, even though the customer volunteered the answer twice: 'the mattress that you're bringing from spare haven to pre andi will go upstairs at my house' and 'her little hall upstairs.' A slay bed frame and mattress going up a flight is the single biggest time variable on this job and it was never priced or discussed.
No special-considerations probe — no long walks, narrow hallways, or tight turns. Getting a slay bed up a staircase is exactly the scenario this bullet exists for.
No access/parking probe at either residence, on a job that involves staging an Einstein truck plus the customer's U-Haul at two separate houses.
Never asked the moving-stressor question — no 'is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?'
No 'pricing is super simple' framing. Jack went straight to 'hourly rate is just $202 an hour for the two movers.'
No what's-included list at all — gas, truck, taxes, insurance, wrap, pads, bands, tools were never named. He gestured at it with 'we're all just time based' but never itemized what the hourly buys.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned — the most glaring miss on this call, because Jack spent his longest single turn on liability: 'it's against our policy to load third party vehicles... we normally just need a waiver that says we are not liable once this, you know, leaves.' He explained what Einstein is NOT liable for without ever explaining what it IS liable for. That is a coverage conversation that ends on the negative half.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned — and he handed himself the setup by quoting a window: 'it'd be a 1:30 to 330 arrival time.' The guarantee is the natural next sentence and it never came.
No 'no hidden fees' pitch — no credit card fees, no transportation fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees.

Clock mechanics mostly absent. He gave the minimum only as a dollar figure ('The minimum is $505') and never said the clock starts on-site when the contract opens, and never explained 15-minute prorated increments after the minimum — on a job he himself said could land near the minimum, where every 15 minutes is the difference between $505 and $707.

Truck count never stated. 'Two movers' was confirmed but never a truck, which is genuinely ambiguous on this job because the customer's own U-Haul is also in the mix. She does not know from this call whether an Einstein truck is showing up.
Drive time between the two addresses (Spire Haven and 6222 Preston) was never named as a factor in the estimate, on a two-location job where the leg between houses is billable clock.
Traffic never mentioned as a variable, despite a 1:30–3:30 PM DFW arrival window on a two-stop job.
Walk distance never asked or mentioned at either address.

The entire Save Your Ass prep speech was skipped. No 'prep before move day = shorter move = lower bill.' This is the highest-leverage miss for a customer whose bill is purely hourly and who was told she might beat the estimate — and there was concrete prep to name: have the U-Haul on site and open, have bungee straps ready, have both rooms cleared and beds stripped, have the waiver signed before the crew arrives. No sense-check close either, because there was no speech to close.
'No deposit required' never mentioned.

Email handoff was announced but not explained — 'I'll go ahead and send you a confirmation email now' with no BOLDED-details framing and no 'reply with any corrections.' That omission is materially risky here: the confirmation is carrying a three-leg bed swap, a third-party U-Haul load, and a liability waiver, all reconstructed from an email Jack had to go dig out of another branch's inbox.

Hours and how to reach us never given — the biggest missed layup on the call. The whole first two minutes existed because her email went to the wrong place ('I just went to in info... it doesn't give you a choice to choose') and Jack diagnosed it himself ('the email probably went to the Dallas location'). He never told her where to send things next time or how to reach him directly.
Customer's name used once, in 'Is this anna?' — never again across a 6.4-minute call with a repeat customer whose name he explicitly said he recognized. Short of the 3+ standard.
Effective insurance explanation missed entirely — no No Worries, no 60¢/lb baseline, on the one call in the batch where a waiver-and-liability discussion actually happened.

Clarity and pace: heavy self-correction and audible thinking-out-loud throughout — 'we're not what we are, we, we're not moving the entire house', 'Yeah, and kind of the crew. There you go', and 'Sorry, I'm thinking out loud as I read through this.' Reading the file out loud to the customer works as transparency but reads as unprepared.

Unscoped work accepted without a time or price adjustment: the customer added 'if she has any furniture in that room or you know book shelves and her little hall upstairs that you all would be helpful, happy to help her move it around,' and Jack agreed — 'if there's a few other yeah, any other furniture swaps, the move, the moves can be really easy for the guys anyways.' Open-ended add-on work on an hourly job, agreed to without a word about how it affects the clock or the estimate.
top_strength: Jack did the unglamorous thing that actually protects a job: he refused to make the customer repeat herself. She had submitted twice, apologized for it ('sorry about that kind of convoluted submissions. I hadn't bought the whole thing all the way through'), and Jack not only found the right submission ('I went deleted the first one. It just jumped into the second one') but then went hunting through a different branch's inbox to find her long explanatory email — 'let me just go check their inbox real fast... just give me half a second and see if I can pull that email up then I don't have to ask you the same questions over and over again.' He then read the plan back to her out loud until she confirmed it, and she said 'That makes Perfect Sense.' On a three-leg bed swap reconstructed from a bad intake, getting the scope right was the whole ballgame and he got it right. The second real strength is how he handled the U-Haul: instead of either refusing or quietly overpromising, he gave her the honest policy and the honest workaround in one turn — 'technically it's against our policy to load third party vehicles we're happy to help. I just, we just can't leave any of our like, Bunge or straps or like equipment on it... we normally just need a waiver.' That is the right instinct: name the boundary, then solve inside it. He was also genuinely budget-honest, quoting the conservative block and then volunteering the upside — 'I would just block off of a four hour block for you. But realistically I think, we can probably get closer to the minimum.' The customer closed with 'Sounds great, appreciate you always,' which is the tell.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Jack talked about liability for four straight sentences and never once said what Einstein covers. Right after 'we normally just need a waiver that says we are not liable once this leaves,' the line he needed was: 'And to be clear on the other side of that — everything we carry on our truck is protected by our No Worries Damage Coverage, up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace, or reimburse accidental damage. The waiver only applies to what goes on your U-Haul, because we can't control how that gets driven.' As it stands, the only insurance content this customer heard was Einstein disclaiming responsibility. Rule to drill: never end a liability sentence on the exclusion — always land on the coverage. Second priority is the Save Your Ass speech, which is worth real money on this specific job. Jack told her she might beat his estimate and then gave her nothing to act on. He should have said: 'Ana, since this is all hourly, here's how you shave time off the bill — have the U-Haul parked, unlocked and empty when we get there, have your bungee straps out and the waiver signed, strip the bedding off both mattresses, and clear a path from each bedroom to the door. That kind of prep can be the difference between the three-and-a-half hours I quoted and hitting the $505 minimum. Does that make sense?' Third: the stairs. She said twice that a mattress is going upstairs and he never acknowledged it or built it into the estimate. Every quote needs 'is anything going up or down stairs at either place?' before a number leaves his mouth, because on a slay bed that answer can move the estimate by an hour. Two business risks to close in EMMA today: (1) Jack verbally agreed to load a third-party U-Haul contingent on a signed liability waiver and the customer supplying her own straps — none of that is confirmed as logged on the job, and if the waiver isn't in hand on Wednesday the crew is either refusing work the branch manager already promised or loading uninsured. Get the waiver requirement and the customer-supplied-straps note onto the job now. (2) He agreed to open-ended extra furniture rearranging at the Spire Haven address on an hourly job with no scope or clock caveat; the job notes should say the add-on work is billable time so nobody is surprised at the invoice. Finally, an easy operational win: the entire first third of this call was Jack recovering from her email landing in the wrong inbox. He diagnosed it correctly and then never told her where to send things. Repeat customers should always leave the call with a direct number and the branch's hours.
phone_presence_notes: Genuinely warm and reassuring with a repeat customer — he defused her apology three separate ways ('Hey. Yeah, I saw you. You're good. Don't worry about it'), personalized it with 'I remember the name, it didn't show up as a repeat number but it definitely I remember,' and she closed with 'appreciate you always'; held back from a 5 only by the constant self-correction and thinking-out-loud that made him sound unprepared for a call he had the file for.

There you go.', 'boots can be pretty easy', 'put that slap at your house on to the trailer').
